medical.title: Common epilepsy medication and birth control combinations may reduce contraceptive effectiveness
medical.summary: Nearly one-third of people with epilepsy who were prescribed certain hormonal contraceptives also received antiseizure medications that may make those contraceptives less effective, according to a University of Pittsburgh–led study published in Neurology.

medical.title: Recordings from hidden brain region reveal clues to how we handle uncertainty
medical.summary: The claustrum is a thin sheet of neurons buried deep within the cerebral cortex. The structure is so small and hidden that neuroscientists once found it very difficult to access, let alone investigate. Now, researchers at Yale School of Medicine have not only found a way to peer into this enigmatic structure but have also discovered its surprising role in how humans learn and adapt to uncertainty.

medical.title: Phthalate byproduct affects multiple cell types in human ovarian tissue, lab tests show
medical.summary: Common chemicals called phthalates, which are used in plastics, cosmetics and personal care products, may affect several different cell types in the human ovary. This is shown in a new study from Karolinska Institutet published in the journal eBioMedicine.

medical.title: How your brain keeps learning while you rest
medical.summary: When you're stuck on a tough problem, it's not uncommon to take a walk or give your brain a break, only to gain that sudden flash of inspiration or insight you were looking for.

medical.title: IVF-conceived children show more 'jumping gene' DNA, study finds
medical.summary: Infertility affects more than 15% of couples worldwide. Thanks to medical science, infertility treatments have come a long way over the past few years. For millions of people, in vitro fertilization (IVF) has opened a medical pathway to having biological children. This procedure gives fertilization a helping hand outside the body. It involves retrieving eggs from the ovaries and fertilizing them with sperm in a laboratory to create embryos.

medical.title: Parasitic worms could hold the key to treating immune system diseases
medical.summary: For millions of years, parasitic worms have had to survive inside animals without being destroyed by their hosts' immune systems. To do that, they have evolved remarkably effective ways of dampening the immune response.

medical.title: Study may explain why IBD patients react to foods they once tolerated
medical.summary: A new study, to be published in Gastroenterology, finds that gut inflammation can change the way gut bacteria break down food—possibly triggering immune reactions to foods that were previously fine to eat. The findings may help explain why so many people with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) react badly to foods like dairy or gluten, even in remission.

medical.title: Brain immune cells protect neurons in Parkinson's disease by 'nibbling' harmful material
medical.summary: Researchers at the University of Oxford have uncovered a previously unrecognized protective role for microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, in Parkinson's disease. The study shows that a distinct population of human microglia can selectively remove harmful clumps (aggregates) of the Parkinson's-causing protein alpha-synuclein from dopamine-producing neurons. The research is published in the journal Science Translational Medicine.

medical.title: Human lung organoids with a built-in immune system could transform respiratory disease research
medical.summary: A new organoid model built with human lung fragments may help us answer key questions about one of the body's first lines of defense against respiratory pathogens. In a new study, researchers at the Stanford University School of Medicine elicited virus-specific immune responses from these organoids and showed that administering a virus booster weakened subsequent infections.

medical.title: Russian plague scare: An expert explains what we know so far—and why there's no need to panic
medical.summary: A laboratory worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in Siberia, Russia, has died just days after falling ill with an undisclosed illness.

medical.title: Rapid low-cost diagnosis within reach for tuberculosis 'missed millions,' researchers find
medical.summary: These findings were generated by the largest-ever study of "pooled" tuberculosis (TB) testing, carried out by Start4All, a partnership led by LSTM with the Stop TB Partnership and research partners in seven countries with a high TB burden.

medical.title: Helping others linked to younger-looking adult brains, even after accounting for health and lifestyle
medical.summary: Population surveys and research studies suggest that meaningful social connections are strong predictors of health and longevity. In other words, a sense of belonging to a social group and strong social bonds appear to be linked with better health and a longer lifespan.

medical.title: One year after taking ibogaine, veterans find continued relief from PTSD
medical.summary: A few years ago, 30 special forces veterans suffering for years with the psychiatric consequences of multiple traumatic brain injuries—including post-traumatic stress disorder, depression and anxiety—traveled to Mexico to undergo a little-known psychedelic therapy called ibogaine.

medical.title: Heart procedures with shielding show uterine radiation well below pregnancy limit, study finds
medical.summary: When female physicians are expecting a child, blanket bans on certain activities—such as surgeries and examinations involving X-rays—are often imposed. This suspension frequently results in a career setback. "For many of our female colleagues, this is a major issue. They enjoy their work, simply want to continue their current duties, or do not want to have to interrupt their specialty training," explains Dr. David Duncker, director of the Hannover Heart Rhythm Center (HHC).

medical.title: Two medications demonstrated comparable results in treating compulsive sexual behavior disorder
medical.summary: Naltrexone and fluoxetine demonstrated similar results in the treatment of people with compulsive sexual behavior disorder in a new study from Karolinska Institutet. Published in BMJ Mental Health, the study found no clear differences between the medications after eight weeks of treatment, although symptom patterns changed differently over time.

medical.title: Experimental cancer treatment disrupts cell communication to suppress tumor growth in animal tests
medical.summary: A research team has developed an anticancer treatment platform that simultaneously targets cancer cells and the surrounding cells that support them while blocking communication between the two.

medical.title: Clinical trial tests AI-assisted medication device for older adults with memory loss
medical.summary: Marianne Blake has lived in the same home for nearly half a century. She plays bridge regularly, drives to her hair appointments and, at 88 years old, enjoys her independence.

medical.title: 'Herd-Immunity-on-a-Chip' recreates viral transmission within a simulated population
medical.summary: A research team led by Professor Sungsu Park of the School of Mechanical Engineering and Professor Byung Mook Weon of the School of Advanced Materials Science and Engineering at Sungkyunkwan University (SKKU) has developed a compact, centimeter-scale microfluidic "Herd-Immunity-on-a-Chip" platform that recreates key features of viral transmission in human societies within a controllable laboratory system.

medical.title: Years of opioid use do not improve chronic back pain, study finds
medical.summary: Taking opioids for years does not seem to reduce pain or improve functioning in people with chronic back pain, according to a new Northwestern University study that compared 70 long-term opioid users with 70 similar patients not taking opioids.

medical.title: Improving early detection of cognitive impairment in primary care
medical.summary: Early detection of cognitive impairment can connect patients with evaluation and treatment sooner, but many screening methods are difficult to incorporate into routine primary care. A study led by Regenstrief Institute research scientist Arthur Owora, Ph.D., MPH, evaluated a scalable approach that combines electronic health record data with a brief patient questionnaire to identify patients who may benefit from further cognitive assessment.

medical.title: Survey participants less likely to recommend life-sustaining care for patients with dementia, despite documented wishes
medical.summary: People were about 19 percentage points less likely to recommend life-sustaining treatment for a seriously ill patient with dementia than for a patient without dementia, even when an advance directive requested life-sustaining care, according to new research from the University of Colorado Anschutz.

medical.title: Health records link ADHD to more than fourfold higher risk of later cognitive impairment
medical.summary: A new study led by University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine researchers finds that adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) face a significantly higher risk of developing dementia or mild cognitive impairment later in life. The research, published today in JAMA Psychiatry, also found that people who carry a higher genetic risk for ADHD face a greater chance of cognitive decline even without a documented diagnosis.

medical.title: Key driver of aggressive prostate cancer identified, suggesting new way to reverse drug resistance
medical.summary: Researchers at Fred Hutch Cancer Center have identified a previously overlooked molecular regulator that helps determine whether prostate tumors remain sensitive to treatment or evolve into a more aggressive, drug-resistant form of the disease.

medical.title: Glucosamine, a popular joint supplement, linked to faster Alzheimer’s progression
medical.summary: A large health-record analysis found that glucosamine use was associated with a 25% higher likelihood of mild cognitive impairment progressing to dementia. Lab experiments suggest the popular joint supplement may intensify an abnormal sugar-tagging process in the Alzheimer’s brain, although researchers say clinical trials are needed to determine whether it actually causes harm.

medical.title: Atrial fibrillation patients saw 69% lower risk with common blood thinners
medical.summary: Direct oral anticoagulants cut the risk of serious clinical events by 69% in atrial fibrillation patients with an intermediate risk of stroke, according to the randomized SINGLE-AF trial. The benefit was driven mainly by fewer ischemic strokes, with no increase in major bleeding.

science.title: Coach training leaves gaps in addressing girls' and women's needs in sport
science.summary: "There is a systemic failure in the training of coaches for female athletes," says Ådne Ausland, a researcher at the University of Agder.

science.title: Cutting unnecessary tasks shows surprising links to greater employee exhaustion
science.summary: Ahead of World Mental Health Day on Oct. 10, attention is turning to the question of what causes psychological strain at work. A study by Bielefeld University shows that inappropriate tasks are not the only factor associated with exhaustion. Changes in day-to-day work can also leave employees feeling exhausted, even when the number of burdensome tasks decreases. Perceived uncertainty plays an important role.

science.title: Polymer coating tackles MXene's water stability challenge, boosting CO₂-to-methane production
science.summary: A research team has developed a photocatalytic technology that improves the stability of MXene, an emerging material vulnerable to water, to efficiently convert carbon dioxide into methane.

science.title: Radio galaxy from 12.5 billion years ago may be most powerful ever found
science.summary: Astronomers have confirmed a powerful radio galaxy from nearly 12.5 billion years ago. The source, TXS 2354+015, was originally identified as a high-redshift candidate from its characteristic drop in optical light, and follow-up spectroscopy placed it at a redshift of 4.946. Their paper was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Sept. 23.

science.title: Enzymes could unlock biological recycling of difficult plastic waste
science.summary: They are durable, cheap and everyday life is now hardly imaginable without them: plastics. More then 400 million metric tons are produced every year. As a large proportion is only insufficiently recycled, the environmental burden caused by plastic waste is increasing.

science.title: Small Michigan communities feel early voting strain
science.summary: Most Michigan city and township officials report positive or neutral impacts from recent state election administration reforms, but many cite the costs and staffing demands associated with nine days of early in-person voting as a concern, according to a new University of Michigan survey.

science.title: Boosting seawater alkalinity could help communities tackle local carbon emissions, researchers argue
science.summary: When scientists discovered that increasing the ocean's natural alkalinity could enhance seawater's capacity to absorb and store carbon dioxide (CO₂), the idea quickly gained attention as a potential geoengineering solution to climate change. Early visions suggested it could remove gigatonnes of CO₂ from the atmosphere each year. But the reality is far more complex.

science.title: As voters weigh incumbents, research complicates case for congressional term limits
science.summary: Most voters see Congress through floor debates, campaign promises and partisan conflict. Yet about half the work done by the average congressional office involves helping constituents, businesses, nonprofits, universities and local governments navigate federal agencies.

science.title: The internal chemistry of phytoplankton changes as oceans become more acidic
science.summary: Our oceans are becoming more acidic, which could have major consequences for marine life. Of particular concern is what this could mean for phytoplankton, the microscopic photosynthetic organisms that form the basis of marine food webs and produce roughly half of the oxygen on Earth. Now, a study published in Nature Geoscience has found that the carbon dioxide we pump into the atmosphere is changing their internal chemistry.

science.title: A honey trap: Female-baited beetle traps reveal habitat variation in Japanese forests
science.summary: Monitoring biological indicators plays a crucial role in forest management, which requires finding a delicate balance between timber use and biodiversity conservation. Across forests and species, responses to forestry operations that alter habitat conditions vary, so repeatable surveys of biological indicators like ground-dwelling beetles can capture spatial variation in forests and changes over time.

science.title: Scientists uncover how the world's smallest flowering plant became so tiny
science.summary: A new study has revealed how some plants pack the same structures as larger species into a tiny space, making them promising candidates for future crops.

science.title: First observation of quantum spins shifting a centimeter-scale object in the lab
science.summary: Modern technological breakthroughs like lasers, MRI scanners, semiconductors and quantum computers rest on the study of quantum mechanics. However, the field has predominantly focused on (sub)atomic phenomena far removed from our human senses.

science.title: 194-year-old tortoise reveals stable gene switches that may help resist aging
science.summary: Researchers studying a giant tortoise named Jonathan say it's not just good genes but a lack of genetic wear and tear that has kept him going for nearly two centuries.

science.title: Ancient spotted bat samples help researchers understand present-day population dynamics
science.summary: Understanding changes in North American bat populations is critical to measuring the risk of extinction from emerging threats such as habitat loss, climate change, white-nose syndrome and other disturbances. A study published Oct. 7, 2026, in the journal PLOS One by Faith M. Walker of Northern Arizona University in the U.S. and colleagues describes a research design involving the genetic analysis of ancient, modern and contemporary biological samples from North American spotted bats.

science.title: Public health strategies used against cigarettes could help reduce appeal of firearms, paper argues
science.summary: Public health strategies that helped reduce cigarette smoking in the United States could provide a model for reducing the appeal and use of firearms, particularly handguns, according to a new paper from the Annenberg Public Policy Center (APPC) of the University of Pennsylvania.

science.title: Dogs and owners disturb each other in the night, but still get pretty good sleep
science.summary: Sleeping alongside your dog probably doesn't disrupt your sleep as much as you might think, according to a study published Oct. 7, 2026, in the journal PLOS One by Ming Fei Li of the University of Toronto, Canada, Lavania Nagendran of the University of Toronto Mississauga, Canada, and colleagues.

science.title: Can picking up a book really improve your brain?
science.summary: Picking up a book for half an hour may feel like simple downtime, but reading for pleasure appears to do more than just entertain us. Research suggests it can support aspects of cognition and well-being, while also helping us understand and connect with other people.

science.title: Seafloor sediments reveal how East Antarctic ice temporarily halted its retreat and advanced 40 miles
science.summary: Off the coast of East Antarctica, researchers led by Kiel University (CAU) and the Alfred Wegener Institute, Helmholtz Centre for Polar and Marine Research (AWI), have investigated an exceptionally large sedimentary body embedded in the seafloor of Vincennes Bay: a so-called "grounding-zone wedge"—symmetrical, wedge-shaped, approximately 260 meters (853 feet) high and 65 kilometers (40 miles) long. With a volume of more than 580 cubic kilometers (139 cubic miles), it is the largest known isolated grounding-zone wedge on a glaciated continental shelf to date and constitutes an exceptional archive of East Antarctica's glacial history.

science.title: Deep-sea clams adjust bacterial partnerships to cope with dwindling chemical energy
science.summary: A research team led by professor Qian Peiyuan, chair professor in the Department of Ocean Science at The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST), in collaboration with international partners, has made progress in uncovering how deep-sea chemosynthetic symbioses cope with environmental change.

science.title: Coolcations: Tourism boom is taking a toll on chillier destinations
science.summary: Rising numbers of visitors headed for destinations in northern Europe in the summer of 2026, seeking respite from the heat.

science.title: NASA’s Curiosity Looks Back After Reaching Elevation Milestone
science.summary: Description NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover captured this view looking back at the floor of Gale Crater, with the crater’s rim visible in the distance, on Sept. 5, 2026, the 5,006th Martian day, or sol, of the mission. Just nine days prior, on Aug. 26 (Sol 4,996), Curiosity set a mission milestone by reaching 1 kilometer […]

science.title: A new hope for dogs with dementia: Researchers explore gene therapy
science.summary: The moment Kate Heath saw her 12-year-old pug, Ivy, sitting silently and staring at a wall, she knew something was wrong.

science.title: One quantum material, two superconducting states: Stretching helps explain conflicting experiments
science.summary: Unconventional superconductors can host unusual electronic states, but understanding what drives their superconductivity becomes difficult when different forms of order coexist. The kagome metal CsV3Sb5 has become a particularly debated example.

science.title: NASA’s Curiosity Captures Dawn Breaking on Wind-Carved Cliffs
science.summary: Description NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover captured this panorama of sunrise illuminating distant, wind-carved features called yardangs on Aug. 11, 2026, the 4,982nd Martian day, or sol, of the mission. Scientists are eager to learn more about how the yardang layer formed. Figure A is a crop zooming in on the distant yardangs. Since 2014, Curiosity […]

science.title: Levitating glass sphere becomes entangled with light at room temperature
science.summary: Today, many physicists are actively exploring how light could be used to link objects through quantum entanglement. By fully harnessing the effect, they hope to unlock a wide array of applications, from secure communication networks spanning vast distances to sensitive new tests of the fundamental laws of physics.

environment.title: New soil test could reveal how soil microbes help feed plants
environment.summary: Scientists have streamlined a method for measuring DNA-bound phosphorus in soil, making it cheaper and easier while preserving its accuracy. The technique could reveal how soil microbes help recycle phosphorus and ultimately support more sustainable fertilizer and nutrient management.

environment.title: 1.7-billion-year-old fossils reveal a crucial clue to the rise of complex life
environment.summary: Scientists studying ancient Australian rocks uncovered more than 12,000 fossils from some of the oldest known eukaryotes on Earth. These early complex cells lived in settings ranging from coastal mudflats to the open sea, but only where oxygen was available. Oxygen-free environments contained simpler microbes instead. The findings strengthen the idea that oxygen played a crucial role in the emergence of complex life.

environment.title: These medieval graves looked like family burials. DNA told a different story
environment.summary: Ancient DNA shows that adults and children buried together in medieval Sweden were often not members of the same immediate family, suggesting that burial choices reflected more than biological kinship. The research also revealed early gender-based burial customs and uncovered the remarkable story of a young woman who may have completed a pilgrimage across Europe.

environment.title: This new concrete is stronger and pulls CO2 from the air
environment.summary: Researchers have created a concrete mixture that is both stronger and capable of absorbing carbon dioxide. The best formula, combining zeolite with bamboo biochar, boosted compressive strength by 7.48% and tensile strength by 15% compared with conventional concrete. It also captured about 1.2 grams of CO₂ per day in laboratory testing.

environment.title: A strange circle on satellite maps turned out to be a 390-million-year-old impact crater
environment.summary: An amateur astronomer searching satellite maps for a Quebec camping spot accidentally discovered a massive ancient impact crater. Scientists later found shatter cones that confirmed the 25-kilometer-wide structure was blasted into Earth roughly 390 million years ago.

mix_items.title: Common epilepsy medication and birth control combinations may reduce contraceptive effectiveness
mix_items.summary: Nearly one-third of people with epilepsy who were prescribed certain hormonal contraceptives also received antiseizure medications that may make those contraceptives less effective, according to a University of Pittsburgh–led study published in Neurology.

mix_items.title: Cutting unnecessary tasks shows surprising links to greater employee exhaustion
mix_items.summary: Ahead of World Mental Health Day on Oct. 10, attention is turning to the question of what causes psychological strain at work. A study by Bielefeld University shows that inappropriate tasks are not the only factor associated with exhaustion. Changes in day-to-day work can also leave employees feeling exhausted, even when the number of burdensome tasks decreases. Perceived uncertainty plays an important role.

mix_items.title: Polymer coating tackles MXene's water stability challenge, boosting CO₂-to-methane production
mix_items.summary: A research team has developed a photocatalytic technology that improves the stability of MXene, an emerging material vulnerable to water, to efficiently convert carbon dioxide into methane.

mix_items.title: Radio galaxy from 12.5 billion years ago may be most powerful ever found
mix_items.summary: Astronomers have confirmed a powerful radio galaxy from nearly 12.5 billion years ago. The source, TXS 2354+015, was originally identified as a high-redshift candidate from its characteristic drop in optical light, and follow-up spectroscopy placed it at a redshift of 4.946. Their paper was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Sept. 23.

mix_items.title: Enzymes could unlock biological recycling of difficult plastic waste
mix_items.summary: They are durable, cheap and everyday life is now hardly imaginable without them: plastics. More then 400 million metric tons are produced every year. As a large proportion is only insufficiently recycled, the environmental burden caused by plastic waste is increasing.

mix_items.title: Recordings from hidden brain region reveal clues to how we handle uncertainty
mix_items.summary: The claustrum is a thin sheet of neurons buried deep within the cerebral cortex. The structure is so small and hidden that neuroscientists once found it very difficult to access, let alone investigate. Now, researchers at Yale School of Medicine have not only found a way to peer into this enigmatic structure but have also discovered its surprising role in how humans learn and adapt to uncertainty.

mix_items.title: Phthalate byproduct affects multiple cell types in human ovarian tissue, lab tests show
mix_items.summary: Common chemicals called phthalates, which are used in plastics, cosmetics and personal care products, may affect several different cell types in the human ovary. This is shown in a new study from Karolinska Institutet published in the journal eBioMedicine.

mix_items.title: Small Michigan communities feel early voting strain
mix_items.summary: Most Michigan city and township officials report positive or neutral impacts from recent state election administration reforms, but many cite the costs and staffing demands associated with nine days of early in-person voting as a concern, according to a new University of Michigan survey.

mix_items.title: Boosting seawater alkalinity could help communities tackle local carbon emissions, researchers argue
mix_items.summary: When scientists discovered that increasing the ocean's natural alkalinity could enhance seawater's capacity to absorb and store carbon dioxide (CO₂), the idea quickly gained attention as a potential geoengineering solution to climate change. Early visions suggested it could remove gigatonnes of CO₂ from the atmosphere each year. But the reality is far more complex.

mix_items.title: How your brain keeps learning while you rest
mix_items.summary: When you're stuck on a tough problem, it's not uncommon to take a walk or give your brain a break, only to gain that sudden flash of inspiration or insight you were looking for.

mix_items.title: IVF-conceived children show more 'jumping gene' DNA, study finds
mix_items.summary: Infertility affects more than 15% of couples worldwide. Thanks to medical science, infertility treatments have come a long way over the past few years. For millions of people, in vitro fertilization (IVF) has opened a medical pathway to having biological children. This procedure gives fertilization a helping hand outside the body. It involves retrieving eggs from the ovaries and fertilizing them with sperm in a laboratory to create embryos.

mix_items.title: As voters weigh incumbents, research complicates case for congressional term limits
mix_items.summary: Most voters see Congress through floor debates, campaign promises and partisan conflict. Yet about half the work done by the average congressional office involves helping constituents, businesses, nonprofits, universities and local governments navigate federal agencies.

mix_items.title: The internal chemistry of phytoplankton changes as oceans become more acidic
mix_items.summary: Our oceans are becoming more acidic, which could have major consequences for marine life. Of particular concern is what this could mean for phytoplankton, the microscopic photosynthetic organisms that form the basis of marine food webs and produce roughly half of the oxygen on Earth. Now, a study published in Nature Geoscience has found that the carbon dioxide we pump into the atmosphere is changing their internal chemistry.

mix_items.title: A honey trap: Female-baited beetle traps reveal habitat variation in Japanese forests
mix_items.summary: Monitoring biological indicators plays a crucial role in forest management, which requires finding a delicate balance between timber use and biodiversity conservation. Across forests and species, responses to forestry operations that alter habitat conditions vary, so repeatable surveys of biological indicators like ground-dwelling beetles can capture spatial variation in forests and changes over time.

mix_items.title: Parasitic worms could hold the key to treating immune system diseases
mix_items.summary: For millions of years, parasitic worms have had to survive inside animals without being destroyed by their hosts' immune systems. To do that, they have evolved remarkably effective ways of dampening the immune response.

mix_items.title: Scientists uncover how the world's smallest flowering plant became so tiny
mix_items.summary: A new study has revealed how some plants pack the same structures as larger species into a tiny space, making them promising candidates for future crops.

mix_items.title: First observation of quantum spins shifting a centimeter-scale object in the lab
mix_items.summary: Modern technological breakthroughs like lasers, MRI scanners, semiconductors and quantum computers rest on the study of quantum mechanics. However, the field has predominantly focused on (sub)atomic phenomena far removed from our human senses.

mix_items.title: 194-year-old tortoise reveals stable gene switches that may help resist aging
mix_items.summary: Researchers studying a giant tortoise named Jonathan say it's not just good genes but a lack of genetic wear and tear that has kept him going for nearly two centuries.

mix_items.title: Ancient spotted bat samples help researchers understand present-day population dynamics
mix_items.summary: Understanding changes in North American bat populations is critical to measuring the risk of extinction from emerging threats such as habitat loss, climate change, white-nose syndrome and other disturbances. A study published Oct. 7, 2026, in the journal PLOS One by Faith M. Walker of Northern Arizona University in the U.S. and colleagues describes a research design involving the genetic analysis of ancient, modern and contemporary biological samples from North American spotted bats.

mix_items.title: Study may explain why IBD patients react to foods they once tolerated
mix_items.summary: A new study, to be published in Gastroenterology, finds that gut inflammation can change the way gut bacteria break down food—possibly triggering immune reactions to foods that were previously fine to eat. The findings may help explain why so many people with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) react badly to foods like dairy or gluten, even in remission.

mix_items.title: Brain immune cells protect neurons in Parkinson's disease by 'nibbling' harmful material
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the University of Oxford have uncovered a previously unrecognized protective role for microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, in Parkinson's disease. The study shows that a distinct population of human microglia can selectively remove harmful clumps (aggregates) of the Parkinson's-causing protein alpha-synuclein from dopamine-producing neurons. The research is published in the journal Science Translational Medicine.

mix_items.title: Public health strategies used against cigarettes could help reduce appeal of firearms, paper argues
mix_items.summary: Public health strategies that helped reduce cigarette smoking in the United States could provide a model for reducing the appeal and use of firearms, particularly handguns, according to a new paper from the Annenberg Public Policy Center (APPC) of the University of Pennsylvania.

mix_items.title: Dogs and owners disturb each other in the night, but still get pretty good sleep
mix_items.summary: Sleeping alongside your dog probably doesn't disrupt your sleep as much as you might think, according to a study published Oct. 7, 2026, in the journal PLOS One by Ming Fei Li of the University of Toronto, Canada, Lavania Nagendran of the University of Toronto Mississauga, Canada, and colleagues.

mix_items.title: Human lung organoids with a built-in immune system could transform respiratory disease research
mix_items.summary: A new organoid model built with human lung fragments may help us answer key questions about one of the body's first lines of defense against respiratory pathogens. In a new study, researchers at the Stanford University School of Medicine elicited virus-specific immune responses from these organoids and showed that administering a virus booster weakened subsequent infections.

mix_items.title: Russian plague scare: An expert explains what we know so far—and why there's no need to panic
mix_items.summary: A laboratory worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in Siberia, Russia, has died just days after falling ill with an undisclosed illness.

mix_items.title: Can picking up a book really improve your brain?
mix_items.summary: Picking up a book for half an hour may feel like simple downtime, but reading for pleasure appears to do more than just entertain us. Research suggests it can support aspects of cognition and well-being, while also helping us understand and connect with other people.

mix_items.title: Seafloor sediments reveal how East Antarctic ice temporarily halted its retreat and advanced 40 miles
mix_items.summary: Off the coast of East Antarctica, researchers led by Kiel University (CAU) and the Alfred Wegener Institute, Helmholtz Centre for Polar and Marine Research (AWI), have investigated an exceptionally large sedimentary body embedded in the seafloor of Vincennes Bay: a so-called "grounding-zone wedge"—symmetrical, wedge-shaped, approximately 260 meters (853 feet) high and 65 kilometers (40 miles) long. With a volume of more than 580 cubic kilometers (139 cubic miles), it is the largest known isolated grounding-zone wedge on a glaciated continental shelf to date and constitutes an exceptional archive of East Antarctica's glacial history.

mix_items.title: Rapid low-cost diagnosis within reach for tuberculosis 'missed millions,' researchers find
mix_items.summary: These findings were generated by the largest-ever study of "pooled" tuberculosis (TB) testing, carried out by Start4All, a partnership led by LSTM with the Stop TB Partnership and research partners in seven countries with a high TB burden.

mix_items.title: Helping others linked to younger-looking adult brains, even after accounting for health and lifestyle
mix_items.summary: Population surveys and research studies suggest that meaningful social connections are strong predictors of health and longevity. In other words, a sense of belonging to a social group and strong social bonds appear to be linked with better health and a longer lifespan.

mix_items.title: Deep-sea clams adjust bacterial partnerships to cope with dwindling chemical energy
mix_items.summary: A research team led by professor Qian Peiyuan, chair professor in the Department of Ocean Science at The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST), in collaboration with international partners, has made progress in uncovering how deep-sea chemosynthetic symbioses cope with environmental change.

mix_items.title: Coolcations: Tourism boom is taking a toll on chillier destinations
mix_items.summary: Rising numbers of visitors headed for destinations in northern Europe in the summer of 2026, seeking respite from the heat.

Just nine days prior, on Aug. 26 (Sol 4,996), Curiosity set a mission milestone by reaching 1 kilometer […]

mix_items.title: A new hope for dogs with dementia: Researchers explore gene therapy
mix_items.summary: The moment Kate Heath saw her 12-year-old pug, Ivy, sitting silently and staring at a wall, she knew something was wrong.

mix_items.title: One quantum material, two superconducting states: Stretching helps explain conflicting experiments
mix_items.summary: Unconventional superconductors can host unusual electronic states, but understanding what drives their superconductivity becomes difficult when different forms of order coexist. The kagome metal CsV3Sb5 has become a particularly debated example.

mix_items.title: One year after taking ibogaine, veterans find continued relief from PTSD
mix_items.summary: A few years ago, 30 special forces veterans suffering for years with the psychiatric consequences of multiple traumatic brain injuries—including post-traumatic stress disorder, depression and anxiety—traveled to Mexico to undergo a little-known psychedelic therapy called ibogaine.

mix_items.title: Heart procedures with shielding show uterine radiation well below pregnancy limit, study finds
mix_items.summary: When female physicians are expecting a child, blanket bans on certain activities—such as surgeries and examinations involving X-rays—are often imposed. This suspension frequently results in a career setback. "For many of our female colleagues, this is a major issue. They enjoy their work, simply want to continue their current duties, or do not want to have to interrupt their specialty training," explains Dr. David Duncker, director of the Hannover Heart Rhythm Center (HHC).

mix_items.title: NASA’s Curiosity Captures Dawn Breaking on Wind-Carved Cliffs
mix_items.summary: Description NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover captured this panorama of sunrise illuminating distant, wind-carved features called yardangs on Aug. 11, 2026, the 4,982nd Martian day, or sol, of the mission. Scientists are eager to learn more about how the yardang layer formed. Figure A is a crop zooming in on the distant yardangs. Since 2014, Curiosity […]

mix_items.title: Two medications demonstrated comparable results in treating compulsive sexual behavior disorder
mix_items.summary: Naltrexone and fluoxetine demonstrated similar results in the treatment of people with compulsive sexual behavior disorder in a new study from Karolinska Institutet. Published in BMJ Mental Health, the study found no clear differences between the medications after eight weeks of treatment, although symptom patterns changed differently over time.

mix_items.title: Levitating glass sphere becomes entangled with light at room temperature
mix_items.summary: Today, many physicists are actively exploring how light could be used to link objects through quantum entanglement. By fully harnessing the effect, they hope to unlock a wide array of applications, from secure communication networks spanning vast distances to sensitive new tests of the fundamental laws of physics.

mix_items.title: Experimental cancer treatment disrupts cell communication to suppress tumor growth in animal tests
mix_items.summary: A research team has developed an anticancer treatment platform that simultaneously targets cancer cells and the surrounding cells that support them while blocking communication between the two.

mix_items.title: Clinical trial tests AI-assisted medication device for older adults with memory loss
mix_items.summary: Marianne Blake has lived in the same home for nearly half a century. She plays bridge regularly, drives to her hair appointments and, at 88 years old, enjoys her independence.

mix_items.title: 'Herd-Immunity-on-a-Chip' recreates viral transmission within a simulated population
mix_items.summary: A research team led by Professor Sungsu Park of the School of Mechanical Engineering and Professor Byung Mook Weon of the School of Advanced Materials Science and Engineering at Sungkyunkwan University (SKKU) has developed a compact, centimeter-scale microfluidic "Herd-Immunity-on-a-Chip" platform that recreates key features of viral transmission in human societies within a controllable laboratory system.

mix_items.title: Years of opioid use do not improve chronic back pain, study finds
mix_items.summary: Taking opioids for years does not seem to reduce pain or improve functioning in people with chronic back pain, according to a new Northwestern University study that compared 70 long-term opioid users with 70 similar patients not taking opioids.

mix_items.title: Improving early detection of cognitive impairment in primary care
mix_items.summary: Early detection of cognitive impairment can connect patients with evaluation and treatment sooner, but many screening methods are difficult to incorporate into routine primary care. A study led by Regenstrief Institute research scientist Arthur Owora, Ph.D., MPH, evaluated a scalable approach that combines electronic health record data with a brief patient questionnaire to identify patients who may benefit from further cognitive assessment.

mix_items.title: Survey participants less likely to recommend life-sustaining care for patients with dementia, despite documented wishes
mix_items.summary: People were about 19 percentage points less likely to recommend life-sustaining treatment for a seriously ill patient with dementia than for a patient without dementia, even when an advance directive requested life-sustaining care, according to new research from the University of Colorado Anschutz.

mix_items.title: Health records link ADHD to more than fourfold higher risk of later cognitive impairment
mix_items.summary: A new study led by University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine researchers finds that adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) face a significantly higher risk of developing dementia or mild cognitive impairment later in life. The research, published today in JAMA Psychiatry, also found that people who carry a higher genetic risk for ADHD face a greater chance of cognitive decline even without a documented diagnosis.

mix_items.title: Key driver of aggressive prostate cancer identified, suggesting new way to reverse drug resistance
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Fred Hutch Cancer Center have identified a previously overlooked molecular regulator that helps determine whether prostate tumors remain sensitive to treatment or evolve into a more aggressive, drug-resistant form of the disease.

mix_items.title: Glucosamine, a popular joint supplement, linked to faster Alzheimer’s progression
mix_items.summary: A large health-record analysis found that glucosamine use was associated with a 25% higher likelihood of mild cognitive impairment progressing to dementia. Lab experiments suggest the popular joint supplement may intensify an abnormal sugar-tagging process in the Alzheimer’s brain, although researchers say clinical trials are needed to determine whether it actually causes harm.

mix_items.title: Atrial fibrillation patients saw 69% lower risk with common blood thinners
mix_items.summary: Direct oral anticoagulants cut the risk of serious clinical events by 69% in atrial fibrillation patients with an intermediate risk of stroke, according to the randomized SINGLE-AF trial. The benefit was driven mainly by fewer ischemic strokes, with no increase in major bleeding.

mix_items.title: New soil test could reveal how soil microbes help feed plants
mix_items.summary: Scientists have streamlined a method for measuring DNA-bound phosphorus in soil, making it cheaper and easier while preserving its accuracy. The technique could reveal how soil microbes help recycle phosphorus and ultimately support more sustainable fertilizer and nutrient management.

mix_items.title: 1.7-billion-year-old fossils reveal a crucial clue to the rise of complex life
mix_items.summary: Scientists studying ancient Australian rocks uncovered more than 12,000 fossils from some of the oldest known eukaryotes on Earth. These early complex cells lived in settings ranging from coastal mudflats to the open sea, but only where oxygen was available. Oxygen-free environments contained simpler microbes instead. The findings strengthen the idea that oxygen played a crucial role in the emergence of complex life.

mix_items.title: These medieval graves looked like family burials. DNA told a different story
mix_items.summary: Ancient DNA shows that adults and children buried together in medieval Sweden were often not members of the same immediate family, suggesting that burial choices reflected more than biological kinship. The research also revealed early gender-based burial customs and uncovered the remarkable story of a young woman who may have completed a pilgrimage across Europe.

mix_items.title: This new concrete is stronger and pulls CO2 from the air
mix_items.summary: Researchers have created a concrete mixture that is both stronger and capable of absorbing carbon dioxide. The best formula, combining zeolite with bamboo biochar, boosted compressive strength by 7.48% and tensile strength by 15% compared with conventional concrete. It also captured about 1.2 grams of CO₂ per day in laboratory testing.

mix_items.title: A strange circle on satellite maps turned out to be a 390-million-year-old impact crater
mix_items.summary: An amateur astronomer searching satellite maps for a Quebec camping spot accidentally discovered a massive ancient impact crater. Scientists later found shatter cones that confirmed the 25-kilometer-wide structure was blasted into Earth roughly 390 million years ago.
